questions.question: If a developer modifies a tracked file, executes `git add`, and then makes further changes to the same file before committing, what content will be recorded in the resulting commit?

answerOptions.text: Only the changes made before the `git add` command was executed.
answerOptions.rationale: Git stages a file exactly as it is at the moment the `git add` command is run; subsequent changes remain in the working directory and are considered unstaged.

answerOptions.text: The version of the file as it exists in the working directory at the time of the commit.
answerOptions.rationale: This assumes Git automatically tracks all live changes, but Git requires explicit staging of content for it to be included in a snapshot.

answerOptions.text: A merged version containing both the staged changes and the newer unstaged edits.
answerOptions.rationale: Git does not automatically merge working tree changes into the index during a standard commit operation.

answerOptions.text: The commit will fail because the file is in an inconsistent state between the index and working tree.
answerOptions.rationale: Git allows files to be simultaneously staged and modified; it does not block commits but simply ignores the unstaged portion.

questions.hint: Consider how the staging area (index) acts as a middle step between the working directory and the permanent history.

questions.question: When examining a Git tree object, a submodule entry is distinguished by a specific file mode of ___.
questions.rationale: Git uses the 160000 mode to indicate that a directory entry is a submodule (a commit in another repository) rather than a standard directory (040000) or blob (100644).
questions.hint: This unique mode identifies the entry as a 'Commit' type within the tree structure of the parent repository.

questions.question: Which of the following components are part of the header Git constructs before calculating the SHA-1 hash for a blob object?

answerOptions.text: The object type (e.g., 'blob').
answerOptions.rationale: Every Git object header must begin by identifying its internal type to ensure proper retrieval and processing.

answerOptions.text: The size of the content in bytes.
answerOptions.rationale: The header includes a space-delimited size value to define the length of the data following the header.

answerOptions.text: A null byte character (represented as $\0$).
answerOptions.rationale: Git uses a null byte to terminate the header and separate it from the actual file content.

answerOptions.text: The filename of the original file.
answerOptions.rationale: Blobs are content-addressable and do not store filenames; filenames are instead stored within tree objects.

questions.hint: Think about the metadata required to define a generic data object before its actual content begins.

questions.question: Explain why it is considered a 'Golden Rule' to avoid rebasing commits that have already been pushed to a public repository.

grading.modelAnswer: Rebasing rewrites history by creating new commits with different SHA-1 hashes for the same changes. If these commits were already pushed, other collaborators who have based their work on the original commits will face major integration conflicts, as their history will no longer match the rewritten history on the server.
grading.rationale: Rebasing creates entirely new object identities (hashes); doing this to public history breaks the continuity of work for everyone else using that repository.
requiredAttributes: Mentions that rebasing rewrites history or changes commit hashes.
Explains that other collaborators have already based work on the original hashes.
States that this leads to conflicts or breaks history for others.

misconceptions: Believing rebasing only moves a pointer without changing the commit's identity.
bluffs: Vague statements about 'breaking the code' without mentioning the history/hash mismatch.

questions.hint: Focus on how commit identities (SHA-1) change during a rebase and how that impacts other people's clones.

questions.question: When using the command `git cherry-pick A..B`, which commits are actually applied to the current branch?

answerOptions.text: Every commit from the one immediately following A up to and including B.
answerOptions.rationale: In Git revision ranges, the start of the range (A) is exclusive, while the end (B) is inclusive.

answerOptions.text: Every commit starting from A and ending at B.
answerOptions.rationale: This misconception fails to account for the exclusive nature of the starting point in standard Git range syntax.

answerOptions.text: Only commits A and B, skipping all intermediate history.
answerOptions.rationale: The double-dot syntax indicates a continuous range walk, not a discrete list of specific commits.

answerOptions.text: Only commit A, as B is considered the parent of the range.
answerOptions.rationale: This incorrectly reverses the parent/child relationship and the inclusive/exclusive logic of the command.

questions.hint: Recall how Git interprets the double-dot range syntax regarding the inclusivity of the start and end points.

questions.question: The feature that allows Git to automatically record and reuse the resolution of a merge conflict, so it does not have to be solved manually a second time, is called ___.
questions.rationale: Rerere stands for 'reuse recorded resolution,' a tool that tracks how you resolve conflict hunks and applies those same fixes if the same conflict appears again.
questions.hint: The name of this tool is a shorthand for its primary function of reusing recorded conflict solutions.

questions.question: What happens to new commits created while a repository is in a 'detached HEAD' state?

answerOptions.text: They are created successfully but do not belong to any branch and may eventually be garbage collected.
answerOptions.rationale: Commits in detached HEAD are reachable only by their hash; without a branch pointer to track them, they are 'orphaned' and prone to being cleaned up by Git.

answerOptions.text: They are automatically added to the master branch once the user switches back.
answerOptions.rationale: Git does not automatically merge detached commits; the user must manually create a branch to preserve them.

answerOptions.text: Git prevents the user from making any commits until a branch is checked out.
answerOptions.rationale: Git allows experimental commits in detached HEAD, but warns the user that they are not attached to a branch.

answerOptions.text: They update the tag that was originally checked out to point to the new work.
answerOptions.rationale: Tags are intended to be fixed points in history; they do not move forward with new commits like branch pointers do.

questions.hint: Think about the role of branch pointers as anchors for the reachability of commits.

questions.question: Which of the following are shared among all linked worktrees when using `git worktree`?

answerOptions.text: The main object database.
answerOptions.rationale: All worktrees share the same underlying data store within the `.git` directory.

answerOptions.text: The commit history and all references starting with `refs/`.
answerOptions.rationale: Branches and tags are shared across all worktrees to ensure a consistent view of the project history.

answerOptions.text: The `HEAD` pointer.
answerOptions.rationale: Each worktree must have its own unique `HEAD` to allow checking out different branches simultaneously.

answerOptions.text: The index (staging area).
answerOptions.rationale: Because each worktree has its own working directory, each requires its own index to stage changes independently.

questions.hint: Distinguish between the global project data (objects/refs) and the local state required for a specific working copy.

questions.question: If a push is rejected with a message to 'fetch first,' what does this typically indicate about the state of the remote repository?

answerOptions.text: The remote branch contains commits that do not exist in the local history.
answerOptions.rationale: Git prevents pushes that are not fast-forwards to protect against overwriting other people's work that has been added to the server since the last local fetch.

answerOptions.text: The local user lacks the necessary permissions to write to the repository.
answerOptions.rationale: Permission issues usually result in an 'Access Denied' or 'Forbidden' error rather than a 'fetch first' hint.

answerOptions.text: The server's disk space is full, preventing new objects from being stored.
answerOptions.rationale: Server resource issues produce specific technical errors, whereas 'fetch first' is a standard version control synchronization warning.

answerOptions.text: The local configuration file has an incorrect URL for the 'origin' remote.
answerOptions.rationale: An incorrect URL would prevent any connection to the server, resulting in a 'remote not found' or 'could not resolve host' error.

questions.hint: This error occurs because the server's history has advanced in a way the local machine is not yet aware of.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the `git sparse-checkout` command, and in what scenario would it be most beneficial?

grading.modelAnswer: The command reduces the working tree to only a subset of the tracked files, based on specific patterns or directories. This is most beneficial in massive 'monorepos' where a developer only needs to work on a small part of the project, significantly improving performance and reducing local disk usage.
grading.rationale: Sparse-checkout allows for a partial view of the project files while maintaining a full history, solving performance issues in extremely large repositories.
requiredAttributes: Mentions reducing the working tree to a subset of files.
Identifies that it is used for large repositories/monorepos.
Mentions a benefit such as performance or saved disk space.

misconceptions: Confusing sparse-checkout with a shallow clone (which limits history, not files).
bluffs: Stating it deletes files from the repository permanently.

questions.hint: Focus on the difference between the full set of tracked files and what is actually visible on the user's hard drive.
